html:
The Ho-Chunk, who call themselves Hoocąk, "people of the big voice", are a Siouan-speaking people of Wisconsin and northern Illinois. In 1492 they lived around Green Bay and Lake Winnebago, surrounded by Algonquian peoples such as the Menominee and the Sauk and Meskwaki. By their own tradition the Oto, Iowa and Missouria split from them long ago.

In 1634 the Frenchman Jean Nicolet reached them at Green Bay, one of the first Europeans in the region. Disease and war soon cut their numbers sharply. Later they traded furs with the French and British.

In the 1800s the United States forced them out of Wisconsin, especially after the Black Hawk War of 1832, and moved them again and again: to Iowa, Minnesota, South Dakota and finally Nebraska. Many kept coming back to Wisconsin. Today they form two nations, the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska.
